fields.question: Why view β-OPSD as a case of regularized policy optimization?
fields.answer: Reference and privileged teacher define a geometric target; token-logit distillation replaces expensive policy optimization. β has the derivation's specific role, not arbitrary mixture weight.
fields.example: Same guidance with different regularization yields different effective targets.

fields.question: How does return-to-go differ from a current-token log gap?
fields.answer: It accumulates discounted future gaps, assigning later consequences to current decisions. Longer horizons can add variance and depend on termination; not automatically more accurate.
fields.example: A single early error can cause several later deviations invisible to immediate gap.

fields.question: Does local β-OPSD execute long CoT with its linear-position proxy?
fields.answer: No. Candidate actions and linear returns replace tokens/trajectory positions. Freeze teacher/reference and preserve ordering; proxy results aren't Qwen LoRA evidence.
fields.example: Suffix sums over a few numbers don't demonstrate equivalent credit in real generation.

fields.question: Why combine geometric teacher/reference interpolation with return-to-go?
fields.answer: Interpolation controls target direction/strength; return-to-go controls temporal credit. Vanilla is a specific setting, not proof arbitrary logit averages solve the same objective. Local positions aren't long sequences.
fields.example: How much to trust teacher and how far later errors influence early choices are separate decisions.

fields.question: Why let Relay-OPD teacher briefly take over then return control?
fields.answer: An invalid prefix can trap future learning. Short, budgeted intervention returns to a learnable region while student still acts after handoff.
fields.example: Teacher repairs a few critical steps, then student finishes.

fields.question: How do relayed traces differ from native student rollouts?
fields.answer: Teacher intervention changes action sources and states; log takeover interval and budget. Teacher-assisted success is not autonomous student success.
fields.example: A teacher bypassing a hard step requires separate no-teacher evaluation.

fields.question: How does the Relay state machine prevent budget overrun?
fields.answer: Track cumulative handoff lengths, enforce total and record takeover/return/termination. Local teacher is cached candidate distribution, not real Qwen or eight-GPU training.
fields.example: Once budget is spent, do not start a second handoff.

fields.question: Why not count a relayed trace as purely student on-policy?
fields.answer: Teacher generates intervened actions and changes later student conditioning. It is a mixture. Budget keeps help local and provenance tracks writers. Include teacher cost and don't claim independent success.
fields.example: A student finishing after two teacher steps need not succeed unaided.

fields.question: Why distill an AR teacher on a diffusion student's own decoding path in OPDLM?
fields.answer: Moving to bidirectional denoising can forget learned behavior. Random masks can miss confidence-decoding states. Actual student rollouts reduce mismatch with inference.
fields.example: Train on the reveal order actually visited, not only random masking.

fields.question: Do AR teacher and bidirectional student see the same information at a position?
fields.answer: No. AR teacher scores causal history, student denoises visible unmasked tokens. Align positions and state what each sees instead of treating conditioning differences as quality.
fields.example: Student may see a revealed token to the right while teacher sees only left context.

fields.question: Where should OPDLM compute loss and does teacher update?
fields.answer: Use specified masked/supervised positions, freeze AR teacher and align logits to student trajectories. Mini-suite does not fully convert/train a real bidirectional LM.
fields.example: Including already determined tokens changes denoising supervision.

fields.question: Why distill along actual bidirectional decoding rather than random masks?
fields.answer: Confidence decoding visits different contexts and attention conversion can cause forgetting. Score student-visited states with frozen AR targets while retaining its causal condition. Different visible evidence cannot be equated positionwise arbitrarily.
fields.example: A confidence-first reveal produces contexts random-mask training might never encounter.

fields.question: Why does GKD ask a teacher to score student-generated prefixes?
fields.answer: Teacher paths can be idealized and miss visited errors. Sample student trajectories and ask for full teacher distributions at those prefixes, teaching recovery without only copying demonstrations.
fields.example: Teacher can guide next actions after the student's second step goes wrong.

fields.question: Is GKD student data fraction the same as IPD token mixing?
fields.answer: No. GKD controls training-source mix of fixed and student traces. IPD mixes policies at each state. Dataset mixtures and one-step mixtures generally visit different trajectories.
fields.example: Half the batch from fixed answers is not choosing teacher with 50% probability at every token.

fields.question: Why specify which distribution comes first in GKD KL?
fields.answer: Forward/reverse KL and generalized JSD differ in coverage and concentration. Freeze teacher on identical student prefixes. Candidate teacher distributions aren't real T5 translation/summarization.
fields.example: KL(T||S) and KL(S||T) yield different gradients despite both being KL.

fields.question: Why does same-prefix teacher scoring reach student mistakes better than complete teacher answers?
fields.answer: Fixed teacher trajectories avoid many student errors. Teacher distributions on sampled student prefixes reach those states; data fraction controls fixed/on-policy mixture. Coverage doesn't guarantee teacher recovery or determine divergence choice.
fields.example: A correct demonstration never visits the student's wrong step, while prefix scoring can help from that actual state.

fields.question: Why favor reverse KL in MiniLLM?
fields.answer: Small students may not cover all teacher modes. Reverse KL concentrates on student-supported reliable teacher regions, possibly missing modes. Sharpness isn't always desirable.
fields.example: Learn several reliable phrasings rather than spread over all teacher continuations.

fields.question: What coverage tradeoff separates MiniLLM from forward KL?
fields.answer: Forward emphasizes teacher-mass coverage; reverse follows student-sampled modes. Teacher-mixed sampling and variance reduction also matter; direction alone isn't the full method.
fields.example: Few reliable modes versus many weak modes requires task evaluation.

fields.question: Whose distribution defines MiniLLM reverse-KL expectation?
fields.answer: Student, with explicit teacher-mixed sampling and corrections in practice. Arbitrary fixed teacher text is not a substitute. Local candidates lack real tokenizer, long generation and GPT judging.
fields.example: Scoring teacher solutions with a KL-looking formula doesn't provide student on-policy coverage.

fields.question: How does reverse KL affect small students' treatment of teacher tails?
fields.answer: Student expectation focuses capacity on visited teacher-supported modes; forward KL covers teacher mass. Direction changes gradients and expectation. Preserve teacher-mixed stabilization; candidate checks aren't long-text distillation.
fields.example: A limited student may concentrate on a few reliable phrasings rather than cover every rare teacher expression.

fields.question: Why ask whether the student can complete an AOPD teacher action?
fields.answer: Teacher's favored next step may be beyond student continuation skill. Relative terminal advantage measures usable guidance from existing student rollouts without counterfactual generations.
fields.example: An advanced proof start is not useful if the student cannot continue it.

fields.question: How does AOPD differ from multiplying KL by reward?
fields.answer: It includes a sampled term and full-distribution term under the same unnormalized truncated teacher measure, plus independent leave-one-out returns. Simple reward multiplication loses that estimator structure.
fields.example: Weighting one sampled word doesn't reproduce subtraction of the vocabulary-wide term.

fields.question: Can AOPD clip only the sampled term or replace rollout S with current student?
fields.answer: No. Both terms share the unnormalized truncated teacher measure; denominator is frozen rollout S. Update only Sθ, with groups larger than one for independent LOO. Don't change behavior probabilities across steps.
fields.example: Re-softmax after truncation changes total mass and correspondence between terms.

fields.question: Why do both AOPD terms share a truncated teacher measure?
fields.answer: The estimator combines terms that cancel to measure teacher-action advantage for student continuation. Clipping only one or renormalizing changes the objective. Use other same-prompt rollouts for LOO, with frozen teacher/behavior and no new counterfactual continuations.
fields.example: Evaluate a teacher-preferred opening against the student's actual returns rather than reinforce it solely from teacher likelihood.
